name: Battle of San Jacinto
info: A Texian army under Sam Houston defeated Antonio López de Santa Anna's Mexican force in about 18 minutes at San Jacinto in Texas on 21 April 1836, the last battle of the Texas Revolution, and Santa Anna was captured the next day.

facts.date: 21 April 1836; the fighting lasted 18 minutes, and the killing of fleeing soldiers went on for hours
facts.place: Near Lynch's Ferry on Buffalo Bayou, by the San Jacinto River, in present-day La Porte and Deer Park, Texas
facts.sides: The Texian Army under General Sam Houston, around 800 men (the official count entering battle was 783); the Mexican army under General Antonio López de Santa Anna, around 700 men on 20 April and approximately 1,200 to 1,500 after General Martín Perfecto de Cos arrived with 540 reinforcements on the morning of 21 April
facts.outcome: The Texians overran the Mexican camp. Santa Anna and Cos escaped the field but were captured on 22 and 24 April, and Santa Anna later signed the Treaties of Velasco, under which the Mexican army withdrew south of the Rio Grande.

t: Houston retreated for weeks before the battle, to the displeasure of his troops, and turned on Santa Anna only after a captured courier gave him the positions and plans of the Mexican troops in Texas.
The Texians numbered around 800 against approximately 1,200 to 1,500 Mexicans, yet the fighting lasted 18 minutes, with 650 Mexican soldiers killed against 11 Texians killed and mortally wounded.

The force beaten at San Jacinto was not the bulk of the Mexican army in Texas; about 4,000 more troops under Urrea and Filisola withdrew after Santa Anna ordered a retreat, and Mexico refused to recognise Texas.
dyk: Tejano soldiers in Juan Seguín's company wore playing cards in their hats so that other Texians would not mistake them for Mexican soldiers.
ev: General Cos takes command in Texas and the Siege of Béxar begins; Cos surrenders in December
The Mexican army takes the Alamo after a 90-minute assault
Houston retreats eastward with his army and civilians in the Runaway Scrape
Texian scouts capture a Mexican courier carrying the locations and plans of the Mexican troops
The two armies camp about 500 yards apart near Lynch's Ferry and skirmish
The Texians storm the Mexican camp and win within 18 minutes
Santa Anna is captured; Cos is taken on 24 April
Santa Anna agrees to the Treaties of Velasco and the Mexican army withdraws south of the Rio Grande

sections.background:
General Antonio López de Santa Anna was a proponent of federalism when he helped oust Mexican President Anastasio Bustamante in December 1832. After his election as president in April 1833 he switched to centralist policies that increased the authority of his office. His abrogation of the Constitution of 1824 and abolition of local authority over the state of Coahuila y Tejas became a flashpoint between the central government and its Tejano and Anglo citizens in Texas. Stephen F. Austin, who had urged a break-away state, was kept imprisoned for most of 1834.

In 1835 Santa Anna installed General Martín Perfecto de Cos as military governor of Texas. Cos set up headquarters in San Antonio on 9 October, and the Siege of Béxar followed. Cos raised a white flag on 9 December and signed surrender terms two days later, which removed the occupying Mexican army from Texas. A circular of 30 December, known as the Tornel Decree, declared that foreigners who entered Mexico to join the rebellion were to be treated as pirates and put to death if captured.

The Mexican Army of Operations numbered 6,019 soldiers. Santa Anna crossed the Rio Grande on 16 February 1836 and took Béxar on 23 February. The Convention of 1836 signed the Texas Declaration of Independence on 2 March, and on 6 March the Mexican troops took the Alamo. General José de Urrea secured the Gulf Coast, and Houston learned of the surrender of James Fannin's men on 20 March.
sections.forces:
The Texian Army was commanded by General Sam Houston, whose military authority had been widened on 4 March to cover all Texian land forces. After the fall of the Alamo, volunteers swelled his ranks to about 1,400 men by 19 March, but many deserted during the retreat. Houston feared that his ill-trained and ill-disciplined force was good for only one battle. At Groce's Landing on the Brazos River the army drilled for the first time, and two cannon known as the Twin Sisters arrived from Cincinnati, Ohio. Houston's army at the battle numbered around 800 men; the official count entering battle was 783.

Santa Anna, the president of Mexico, led about 700 men to Lynch's Ferry. On the morning of 21 April Cos arrived with 540 reinforcements, bringing the Mexican force to approximately 1,200 to 1,500. Cos's men were mostly raw recruits and had marched for more than 24 hours without rest or food. A further 4,000 Mexican troops remained under General Urrea and General Vicente Filisola.

Houston's army reached the ferry on 20 April and camped in woods along Buffalo Bayou, which hid its full strength but left no room to retreat. Over the protests of several officers, Santa Anna camped on a plain near the San Jacinto River, bordered by woods on one side and marsh and lake on another, about 500 yards from the Texians. Colonel Pedro Delgado later wrote that the site was against military rules. Houston placed Colonel Edward Burleson in the centre, the second regiment under Colonel Sherman on the left, the artillery under Colonel George W. Hackley on the right with four companies under Lieutenant Colonel Henry Millard, and 61 cavalry under Colonel Mirabeau B. Lamar on the extreme right.
sections.course:
Two brief skirmishes took place on 20 April. The Texians used the Twin Sisters to force a small group of dragoons and the Mexican artillery to withdraw, and Mexican dragoons then forced the Texian cavalry back. Thomas Rusk was almost captured on foot and was rescued by Lamar. Many Texian infantrymen rushed onto the field against Houston's orders, which angered him because it gave Santa Anna a better estimate of their strength. During the night the Mexican troops built breastworks out of saddles, brush and whatever else they could find.

On 21 April, as the morning wore on with no Texian attack, the Mexican officers lowered their guard, and by afternoon Santa Anna had allowed Cos's men to sleep while the rest rested, ate and bathed. Houston had ordered Deaf Smith to destroy Vince's Bridge, about 8 miles from the camp, to block the only road out. The Texian cavalry went to the Mexican left, and the artillery advanced through tall grass to within 200 yards of the breastworks.

The Twin Sisters fired at 4:30 and the battle began. After a single volley the Texians broke ranks and swarmed over the breastworks, shouting "Remember the Alamo! Remember La Bahia (Goliad)!", and fought hand to hand. The Mexican soldiers were taken by surprise. Santa Anna, Castrillón and Almonte shouted conflicting orders. Within 18 minutes the Mexican soldiers had abandoned their camp and fled. Many retreated through the marsh to Peggy Lake, where Texian riflemen shot at anything that moved. Houston, Rusk and other officers tried to stop the killing but could not control men angry over the Alamo and Goliad. The killing lasted for hours.
sections.aftermath:
Historian Davis called the victory one of the most one-sided in history: 650 Mexican soldiers were killed, 208 wounded and 300 captured, while 11 Texians were killed or mortally wounded and 30 wounded, Houston among them with a shot to the ankle. Texian soldiers gathered round the captured Santa Anna, who had fled towards Vince's Bridge, found it destroyed and hidden in the marsh, and called for his execution. He was captured on 22 April wearing a private's jacket, and other prisoners cried out when they recognised him. Cos was captured on 24 April.

Santa Anna wrote to Filisola, now the senior Mexican officer in Texas, that an unfortunate encounter had taken place, and ordered a retreat to Béxar. Urrea urged Filisola to continue the campaign, but Filisola did not wish to risk another disaster. Spring rains had ruined the ammunition and the roads, supplies had broken down and the troops were falling ill with dysentery. The Treaties of Velasco required all Mexican troops to withdraw south of the Rio Grande and Santa Anna to be given passage to Veracruz. In a secret version he promised to persuade the Mexican Congress to recognise Texas and the Rio Grande border.

Many former slaves followed Urrea's army to Mexico, where they could be free, though the treaty required their return. Mexico refused to recognise any agreement signed by a prisoner, and Filisola was replaced by Urrea. The Mexican dead lay unburied on the battlefield for years. Rusk ordered the Tejanos between the Guadalupe and Nueces rivers to move east or to Mexico, and hundreds of Tejano families later resettled in Mexico.
sections.sources:
Houston wrote a detailed first-hand account from the headquarters of the Texian Army at San Jacinto on 25 April 1836, and it gives the order in which he arrayed his troops. Colonel Pedro Delgado of the Mexican army later wrote on Santa Anna's choice of camp, and Filisola wrote afterwards of his troops' plight on the retreat.

Strengths are approximate. The Texian force is put at around 800, with an official count of 783, and the Mexican force at approximately 1,200 to 1,500, a range that includes Cos's 540 reinforcements. The casualty figures are those given by the historian Davis. The mass grave of the Mexican dead has never been located.
sections.legacy:
Houston became a national celebrity, and the cries "Remember the Alamo" and "Remember Goliad" became part of Texian history and legend. Santa Anna's treaties did not necessarily recognise Texas as a sovereign nation but stipulated that he was to lobby for recognition in Mexico City. In the months after the battle so many American volunteers flocked to the Texian army that the government could not keep an accurate list. Voters made Houston the first president of the Republic of Texas, ratified its constitution and approved a request for annexation to the United States.

In Mexico, authorities used the plan to reconquer Texas to justify new taxes and to put the army first in the budget, but larger expeditions were postponed as funds went to other rebellions. The northern Mexican states briefly launched an independent Republic of the Rio Grande in 1839, and in June 1843 leaders of the two nations declared an armistice. Santa Anna was disgraced until the following year, when he became a hero of the Pastry War.

The San Jacinto Battleground State Historic Site was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1960. It holds the 570 ft San Jacinto Monument, authorised on 21 April 1936 and dedicated on 21 April 1939, and holds a San Jacinto Day festival and battle re-enactment each April. The Texas Navy and the United States Navy named ships after the battle, and the battleship USS Texas was anchored near the monument as a museum ship in 1948.

summary: At San Jacinto on 21 April 1836 a Texian army of around 800 under Sam Houston overran the camp of Santa Anna's Mexican force of approximately 1,200 to 1,500 in 18 minutes. Santa Anna was captured and agreed to withdraw his army from Texas, though Mexico refused to recognise Texan independence.
notes: The article's Cos reinforcement (540) plus Santa Anna's 700 gives about 1,240; the article's range is 1,200-1,500 and I kept its wording.
Houston's quotation in the article gives 'Sydney Sherman (sic)' and 'Geo. W. Hackley'; I used 'Colonel Sherman' and 'George W. Hackley' as the article does.
The article's claim that Santa Anna and Houston refused to order burial, and its reasons, is left out as thin and speculative; only the unburied dead and unknown mass grave are kept.
Santa Anna's secret treaty terms and the article's statement that the treaties 'did not necessarily recognize Texas' are given as the article has them.
The article has no real discussion of sources; the sources section is short and describes only what the article names.
The article gives the dates of Almonte's pursuit of the Texian government, Burnet's flight and the burning of Harrisburgh; left out for length.
Left out: ships named San Jacinto beyond one line, Mirabeau Lamar's speech on mobs, and the Texian Navy schooner details.
